Sagacious

suh-GAY-shus · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sagacious is having or showing very sound judgment and sharp insight.

Villagers came from miles away to ask the sagacious elder for advice before making any major decision.

Worked Example

The sagacious old judge saw through the witness's story in seconds, asking exactly the right question to expose the lie.

Seeing through a false story in seconds with exactly the right question is exactly sagacious judgment.

How Sagacious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

clear-sighted

clear-sighted: having sharp, sound practical judgment

astute

astute: showing sharp insight and good judgment

Antonyms

foolish

foolish: lacking good sense or judgment

How Strong Is It? — sensible → prescient → sagacious

sensible vs. sagacious

sensible vs. sagacious: Sensible describes ordinary good judgment that most people show day to day; sagacious describes a rarer, sharper wisdom that impresses others.

prescient vs. sagacious

prescient vs. sagacious: Prescient adds an almost uncanny ability to predict the future, while sagacious stays grounded in clear-sighted judgment about the present.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — sag

root — sag: to perceive keenly (Latin (sagire))

suffix — -acious

suffix — -acious: inclined to, full of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Sagacious comes from Latin sagire ('to perceive sharply') + -acious ('inclined to') -- literally 'inclined to sharp perception.'

Use the root in a new word: seek

Use the root in a new word: seek: Sagire traces back to the same ancient root behind the everyday English word seek -- both carry the idea of tracking something down through careful attention.

Root Check

Word Choice

Sagacious describes a person's sharp, practical judgment -- often about people or situations -- distinct from Astute, which describes a similar quick insight but with less emphasis on accumulated wisdom.
